Anterior horn cells at the level form the LMN pool, whereas descending lateral corticospinal tracts affect everything downstream unilaterally causing spasticity, hyperreflexia, and Babinski sign.

Diagram Labels: Key Structures Shown: ipsilateral • flaccid • spastic

question: Regarding the corticospinal (pyramidal) tracts, {c1::85 - 90%}} of fibers form the lateral corticospinal tract supplying limb muscles, while {c2::10 - 15%}} form the anterior corticospinal tract supplying axial muscles.
answer: Decussation of the pyramids occurs at the lower medulla oblongata.

question: The pyramidal decussation occurs at the lower part of the {c1::medulla oblongata}}.
answer: This explains why cortical lesions result in contralateral motor deficits.

question: On the ventral aspect of the brainstem, the interpeduncular fossa is bounded by the optic chiasma/tract anteriorly, {c1::cerebral peduncles (crus cerebri)}} laterally, and the pons or third ventricle regions accordingly.
answer:
Contents of the interpeduncular fossa include the pituitary gland infundibulum, tuber cinereum, mammillary bodies, CN III, and the posterior perforating substance.

Diagram Labels: Key Structures Shown: cerebral peduncles (crus cerebri) • posterior cerebral artery (PCA) • CN V (Trigeminal) • pyramid • olive • CN IV (Trochlear)

question: The posterior perforating substance found in the interpeduncular fossa is pierced by branches of the {c1::posterior cerebral artery (PCA)}}.
answer:
Supplies deep structures like parts of the midbrain and thalamus.

Diagram Labels: Key Structures Shown: cerebral peduncles (crus cerebri) • posterior cerebral artery (PCA) • CN V (Trigeminal) • pyramid • olive • CN IV (Trochlear)

question: Among all cranial nerves, cranial nerve {c1::CN V (Trigeminal)}} is the thickest.
answer:
Emerges from the lateral aspect of the pons.

Diagram Labels: Key Structures Shown: cerebral peduncles (crus cerebri) • posterior cerebral artery (PCA) • CN V (Trigeminal) • pyramid • olive • CN IV (Trochlear)

question: The hypoglossal nerve (CN XII) exits the medulla oblongata in the sulcus located between the {c1::pyramid}} and the {c2::olive}}.
answer:
Lesion of CN XII produces ipsilateral deviation of the tongue upon protrusion ('Lick the lesion').

Diagram Labels: Key Structures Shown: cerebral peduncles (crus cerebri) • posterior cerebral artery (PCA) • CN V (Trigeminal) • pyramid • olive • CN IV (Trochlear)

question: Cranial nerve {c1::CN IV (Trochlear)}} is unique because it is the only cranial nerve that emerges from the {c2::dorsal}} aspect of the brainstem.
answer:
It supplies the superior oblique muscle and decussates completely before exiting.

Diagram Labels: Key Structures Shown: cerebral peduncles (crus cerebri) • posterior cerebral artery (PCA) • CN V (Trigeminal) • pyramid • olive • CN IV (Trochlear)

question: The facial colliculus on the floor of the IVth ventricle (rhomboid fossa) is formed by the {c1::1st genu of the facial nerve (CN VII)} looping around the {c2::abducens nucleus (CN VI)}.
answer:
Facial colliculus injury affects CN VII more than CN VI nucleus, resulting in an ipsilateral LMN facial paralysis.

Diagram Labels: Key Structures Shown: 1st genu of the facial nerve (CN VII) • abducens nucleus (CN VI)

question: In the mnemonic 'E COLI MA' for the auditory pathway (Lateral Lemniscus), E stands for {c1::Eight cranial nerve (Cochlear nerve)} and CO stands for {c2::Cochlear nucleus}.
answer: Complete pathway: Eight cranial nerve -> Cochlear nucleus -> Trapezoid body (decussates) -> Superior olivary nucleus -> Lateral lemniscus -> Inferior colliculus -> MGB -> Auditory cortex (Area 41, 42).

question: The superior olivary nucleus acts as the center for the {c1::stapedial reflex}.
answer: It receives bilateral auditory input, crucial for dampening loud sounds via contraction of the stapedius muscle.

question: Facial colliculus injury characteristically affects {c1::CN VII} > {c2::CN VI nucleus}, leading to ipsilateral LMN facial paralysis.
answer:
Because the CN VII motor fibers loop directly over the abducens nucleus, a localized lesion here damages both the abducens nucleus and the facial nerve genu.

Diagram Labels: Key Structures Shown: CN VII • CN VI nucleus

question: A lesion of the medial lemniscus (carrying anterior spinothalamic tract and dorsal column tract) results in {c1::contralateral} loss of touch, pressure, vibration, stereognosis, and conscious proprioception.
answer: Medial lemniscus fibers cross the midline in the medulla as internal arcuate fibers, hence lesions above the decussation cause contralateral deficits.

question: Injury to the lateral lemniscus in the brainstem causes {c1::contralateral hearing loss}.
answer: Due to bilateral representation in the auditory ascending pathways, a unilateral lesion causes partial hearing deficits predominantly affecting the contralateral ear.

question: The spinal lemniscus (lateral spinothalamic tract) transmits pain and temperature sensations from below the face, and its lesion leads to {c1::contralateral loss of pain and temperature}.
answer: Fibers cross in the spinal cord white commissure shortly after entering, explaining the contralateral sensory loss upon brainstem tract injury.

question: A lesion of the trigeminal lemniscus results in {c1::contralateral loss of facial sensations}.
answer: Carries secondary trigeminal sensory fibers up to the thalamus (VPM nucleus).

question: A section of the midbrain at the level of the superior colliculus demonstrates the {c1::red nucleus}, {c2::corticospinal tract}, and {c3::corticonuclear tract} (UMN of CN VII).
answer:
Key landmark for Weber's syndrome and Benedikt's syndrome localization in midbrain strokes.

Diagram Labels: Key Structures Shown: red nucleus • corticospinal tract • corticonuclear tract • CN III (Oculomotor nerve)

question: The interpeduncular fossa on the ventral midbrain is the exit site for cranial nerve {c1::CN III (Oculomotor nerve)}.
answer:
Lesions affecting the interpeduncular fossa typically present with ipsilateral CN III palsy combined with contralateral hemiplegia (Weber syndrome).

Diagram Labels: Key Structures Shown: red nucleus • corticospinal tract • corticonuclear tract • CN III (Oculomotor nerve)

question: Benedict's syndrome presents with ipsilateral {c1::CN III palsy} and contralateral loss of touch, vibration, conscious proprioception, stereognosis, and pressure.
answer:
Involves red nucleus and oculomotor nerve fibers in the midbrain/pons junction.

Diagram Labels: Key Structures Shown: CN III palsy • hemiplegia • basilar artery • acoustic neuroma • ipsilateral • corticospinal tract

question: Weber's syndrome is characterized by ipsilateral CN III palsy and contralateral {c1::hemiplegia} along with contralateral paralysis of the lower half of the face.
answer:
Caused by a lesion affecting the crus cerebri and exiting CN III rootlets.

Diagram Labels: Key Structures Shown: CN III palsy • hemiplegia • basilar artery • acoustic neuroma • ipsilateral • corticospinal tract

question: Millard-Gubler syndrome is typically caused by vascular compromise of the {c1::basilar artery} and presents with ipsilateral facial paralysis and contralateral hemiplegia.
answer:
Also features ipsilateral convergent squint due to CN VI involvement.

Diagram Labels: Key Structures Shown: CN III palsy • hemiplegia • basilar artery • acoustic neuroma • ipsilateral • corticospinal tract

question: Lateral pontine syndrome is classically associated with {c1::acoustic neuroma} (vestibular schwannoma) pressing on the lateral pontine structures.
answer:
Presents with ipsilateral facial paralysis, ipsilateral progressive deafness, and contralateral loss of pain and temperature below the face.

Diagram Labels: Key Structures Shown: CN III palsy • hemiplegia • basilar artery • acoustic neuroma • ipsilateral • corticospinal tract

question: In lateral pontine syndrome, loss of pain and temperature sensation from the face is {c1::ipsilateral} due to involvement of the spinal nucleus of the V nerve.
answer:
Contralateral loss affects the body below the face via the spinothalamic/spinal lemniscus tract.

Diagram Labels: Key Structures Shown: CN III palsy • hemiplegia • basilar artery • acoustic neuroma • ipsilateral • corticospinal tract

question: Medial medullary syndrome features ipsilateral tongue paralysis (due to CN XII damage) and contralateral {c1::hemiplegia}.
answer:
Also causes contralateral loss of touch, pressure, vibration, stereognosis, and conscious proprioception.

Diagram Labels: Key Structures Shown: hemiplegia • posterior inferior cerebellar artery (PICA) • contralaterally • corticospinal tract

question: Lateral medullary syndrome (Wallenberg syndrome) is caused by occlusion of the {c1::posterior inferior cerebellar artery (PICA)}.
answer:
Presents with ipsilateral bulbar paralysis (dysphagia, dysarthria, dyspnea) and ipsilateral loss of the gag reflex.

Diagram Labels: Key Structures Shown: hemiplegia • posterior inferior cerebellar artery (PICA) • contralaterally • corticospinal tract

question: In Wallenberg syndrome (lateral medullary syndrome), pain and temperature sensation is lost {c1::contralaterally} below the face.
answer:
Facial pain and temperature loss remains ipsilateral due to spinal trigeminal nucleus involvement.

Diagram Labels: Key Structures Shown: hemiplegia • posterior inferior cerebellar artery (PICA) • contralaterally • corticospinal tract

question: The basilar part of the pons contains the descending {c1::corticospinal tract} fibers.
answer:
Visible anteriorly in transverse sections of the pons.

Diagram Labels: Key Structures Shown: CN III palsy • hemiplegia • basilar artery • acoustic neuroma • ipsilateral • corticospinal tract

question: In a transverse section of the medulla oblongata, the pyramid is located anteriorly and carries the {c1::corticospinal tract} fibers before their motor decussation.
answer:
Medial medullary syndrome directly affects the pyramid and hypoglossal nerve rootlets.

Diagram Labels: Key Structures Shown: hemiplegia • posterior inferior cerebellar artery (PICA) • contralaterally • corticospinal tract

question: The cerebellar cortex is the outer grey matter of the cerebellum and represents the {c1::largest collection of neurons in the CNS}.
answer:
Despite its small size compared to the cerebrum, the cerebellum contains more than half of all neurons in the entire brain.

Diagram Labels: Key Structures Shown: largest collection of neurons in the CNS • Purkinje cells • largest cells

question: The climbing fibres in the cerebellar cortex originate primarily from the {c1::olivocerebellar & para-olivocerebellar tracts}.
answer:
Climbing fibres provide powerful excitatory input directly to the dendrites of Purkinje cells and use glutamate as a neurotransmitter.

Diagram Labels: Key Structures Shown: olivocerebellar & para-olivocerebellar tracts • other cerebellar tracts • granule cell • cerebellar glomeruli

question: Mossy fibres in the cerebellar cortex arise from {c1::other cerebellar tracts} (such as spinocerebellar, vestibulocerebellar, and pontocerebellar tracts).
answer:
Mossy fibres synapse in the granular layer (cerebellar glomeruli) with granule cell dendrites, whose axons ascend to form parallel fibres.

Diagram Labels: Key Structures Shown: olivocerebellar & para-olivocerebellar tracts • other cerebellar tracts • granule cell • cerebellar glomeruli

question: {c1::Purkinje cells} are the only efferent neurons from the cerebellar cortex.
answer:
They are flask-shaped cells located in the Purkinje layer and exert an inhibitory (GABAergic) effect on the deep cerebellar nuclei.

Diagram Labels: Key Structures Shown: largest collection of neurons in the CNS • Purkinje cells • largest cells

question: Regarding the cellular characteristics of the cerebellar cortex, Purkinje cells are the {c1::largest cells} in the cortex.
answer:
Granule cells are the smallest and most numerous cells, located in the innermost granular layer.

Diagram Labels: Key Structures Shown: largest collection of neurons in the CNS • Purkinje cells • largest cells

question: The only excitatory cell type within the cerebellar cortex is the {c1::granule cell}.
answer:
All other intrinsic cortical neurons (basket, stellate, Golgi cells) and Purkinje cells are inhibitory (GABAergic).

Diagram Labels: Key Structures Shown: olivocerebellar & para-olivocerebellar tracts • other cerebellar tracts • granule cell • cerebellar glomeruli

question: Synaptic complexes known as {c1::cerebellar glomeruli} are found in the granular layer of the cerebellar cortex.
answer:
They are specialized synaptic islands containing mossy fibre rosettes, Golgi cell terminals, and granule cell dendrites surrounded by glial cells.

Diagram Labels: Key Structures Shown: olivocerebellar & para-olivocerebellar tracts • other cerebellar tracts • granule cell • cerebellar glomeruli

question: The middle cerebellar peduncle (MCP) is the {c1::largest peduncle} and is {c2::purely afferent}.
answer:
It transmits pontocerebellar fibres arising from pontine nuclei, carrying information originating from the contralateral cerebral cortex (corticopontocerebellar tract).

Diagram Labels: Key Structures Shown: largest peduncle • purely afferent • copy of the corticospinal tract (CST) • superior cerebellar peduncle • dentate nucleus

question: The ventral spinocerebellar tract acts as a {c1::copy of the corticospinal tract (CST)} and is a major tract passing through the {c2::superior cerebellar peduncle}.
answer:
It relays internal feedback regarding spinal motor neuron activity to the cerebellum.

Diagram Labels: Key Structures Shown: largest peduncle • purely afferent • copy of the corticospinal tract (CST) • superior cerebellar peduncle • dentate nucleus

question: The {c1::dentate nucleus} is the largest of the deep cerebellar nuclei.
answer:
Efferents from the dentate nucleus project via the superior cerebellar peduncle to form the dentatothalamic and dentatorubrothalamic tracts targeting the VL nucleus of the thalamus and red nucleus.

Diagram Labels: Key Structures Shown: largest peduncle • purely afferent • copy of the corticospinal tract (CST) • superior cerebellar peduncle • dentate nucleus

question: The cranial-most end of the neural tube corresponds to the {{c1::lamina terminalis}}.
answer:
High Yield: Lamina terminalis forms the anterior wall of the third ventricle and marks the embryonic closure site of the rostral neuropore.

Diagram Labels: Key Structures Shown: lamina terminalis • lateral ventricles • origin • mammillary body

question: The septum pellucidum separates the two {{c1::lateral ventricles}}.
answer:
High Yield: It is a thin, vertical double-membrane located between the anterior horns of the lateral ventricles.

Diagram Labels: Key Structures Shown: lamina terminalis • lateral ventricles • origin • mammillary body

question: The hippocampus serves as the {{c1::origin}} of the fornix, while the {{c2::mammillary body}} serves as its termination.
answer:
High Yield: Part of the Papez circuit involved in emotion and memory. Damage leads to anterograde amnesia.

Diagram Labels: Key Structures Shown: lamina terminalis • lateral ventricles • origin • mammillary body

question: The white matter fibers of the cerebrum are classified into three main types: association fibers, commissural fibers, and {{c1::projection}} fibers.
answer: High Yield: Commissural fibers (e.g., corpus callosum) connect corresponding areas of two hemispheres; projection fibers connect cortex to subcortical structures.

question: The insular cortex (insula) is a hidden gyrus that can be seen upon opening the {{c1::Sylvian sulcus}} (lateral fissure).
answer:
High Yield: Implicated in gustation, visceral sensation, and autonomic control.

Diagram Labels: Key Structures Shown: Sylvian sulcus • corpus callosum • septum pellucidum • lateral • medial • corona radiata

question: In the coronal section, the roof of the lateral ventricle is formed by the {{c1::corpus callosum}} and its medial wall by the {{c2::septum pellucidum}}.
answer:
High Yield: Essential landmarks for interpreting neuroimaging and ventricular anatomy.

Diagram Labels: Key Structures Shown: Sylvian sulcus • corpus callosum • septum pellucidum • lateral • medial • corona radiata

question: The forceps minor connects the bilateral {{c1::frontal}} lobes, whereas the forceps major connects the bilateral {{c2::occipital}} lobes.
answer: High Yield: Both are formed by fibers of the corpus callosum (genu and splenium respectively).

question: The tapetum of the corpus callosum produces the {{c1::bulb of the posterior horn}} of the lateral ventricle.
answer: High Yield: Tapetum consists of fibers passing laterally from the splenium and body of the corpus callosum to the temporal and parietal lobes.

question: The lentiform nucleus is located {{c1::lateral}} to the internal capsule, whereas the thalamus and caudate nucleus are located {{c2::medial}} to it.
answer:
High Yield: Internal capsule carries major ascending and descending tracts (e.g., corticospinal tract).

Diagram Labels: Key Structures Shown: Sylvian sulcus • corpus callosum • septum pellucidum • lateral • medial • corona radiata

question: Fibers of the internal capsule radiate outwards to form the {{c1::corona radiata}} before entering the cerebral cortex.
answer:
High Yield: Corona radiata convergence forms the internal capsule, which then condenses inferiorly into the cerebral peduncles.

Diagram Labels: Key Structures Shown: Sylvian sulcus • corpus callosum • septum pellucidum • lateral • medial • corona radiata

question: The deep cerebellar nuclei from medial to lateral are: Fastigial, Globose, Emboliform, and {{c1::Dentate}}.
answer:
Mnemonic: Don't Eat Greasy Food (Lateral to medial: Dentate, Emboliform, Globose, Fastigial). Globose + Emboliform = Nucleus Interpositus.

Diagram Labels: Key Structures Shown: Dentate • Purkinje cells • GABA

question: The only efferent output of the cerebellar cortex is formed by the axons of {{c1::Purkinje cells}}, which release the inhibitory neurotransmitter {{c2::GABA}}.
answer:
Layers of Cerebellar Cortex:
1. Molecular layer (Stellate, Basket cells).
2. Purkinje cell layer (single row of flask-shaped Purkinje cells).
3. Granular layer (Granule cells - only excitatory cells, Golgi cells).

Diagram Labels: Key Structures Shown: Dentate • Purkinje cells • GABA

question: Climbing fibers of the cerebellum originate exclusively from the {{c1::inferior olivary nucleus}} in the medulla and synapse directly onto Purkinje cell dendrites.
answer:
Afferents to Cerebellum:
- Climbing fibers: Inferior olivary complex (1 climbing fiber excites 1 Purkinje cell with powerful complex spikes).
- Mossy fibers: All other afferents (synapse on Granule cells -> parallel fibers).

Diagram Labels: Key Structures Shown: inferior olivary nucleus • vestibulocerebellar

question: The Inferior Cerebellar Peduncle contains the olivocerebellar tract, dorsal spinocerebellar tract, and the {{c1::vestibulocerebellar}} tract.
answer:
Peduncles Summary:
- Superior: Chiefly efferents (Dentatorubral, Dentatothalamic).
- Middle: Pontocerebellar (cortico-ponto-cerebellar pathway).
- Inferior: Chiefly afferents from spinal cord, medulla, and vestibular system.

Diagram Labels: Key Structures Shown: inferior olivary nucleus • vestibulocerebellar

question: In Wallenberg syndrome (Lateral Medullary Syndrome) caused by occlusion of the {{c1::PICA (Posterior Inferior Cerebellar Artery)}}, the nucleus ambiguus is infarcted, causing {{c2::dysphagia, dysphonia, and loss of gag reflex}}.
answer:
Wallenberg Syndrome Key Findings:
- Nucleus ambiguus (IX, X): Dysphagia, hoarseness, hiccup.
- Spinal tract/nucleus of V: Ipsilateral facial pain/temperature loss.
- Spinothalamic tract: Contralateral body pain/temperature loss.
- Sympathetic tract: Ipsilateral Horner's syndrome.
- Vestibular nuclei: Vertigo, nystagmus.

Diagram Labels: Key Structures Shown: PICA (Posterior Inferior Cerebellar Artery) • dysphagia, dysphonia, and loss of gag reflex • hypoglossal nerve (CN XII)

question: Medial Medullary Syndrome (Dejerine syndrome) is caused by thrombosis of the anterior spinal artery or paramedian branches of vertebral artery, injuring the {{c1::hypoglossal nerve (CN XII)}}, corticospinal tract, and medial lemniscus.
answer:
Triad of Medial Medullary Syndrome:
1. Ipsilateral deviation of tongue on protrusion (CN XII).
2. Contralateral hemiparesis (Corticospinal tract).
3. Contralateral loss of conscious proprioception/vibration (Medial lemniscus).

Diagram Labels: Key Structures Shown: PICA (Posterior Inferior Cerebellar Artery) • dysphagia, dysphonia, and loss of gag reflex • hypoglossal nerve (CN XII)

question: Weber syndrome is a medial midbrain infarction due to posterior cerebral artery paramedian branch occlusion, affecting the {{c1::oculomotor nerve (CN III)}} and {{c2::cerebral peduncle (corticospinal tract)}}.
answer:
Findings in Weber's: Ipsilateral CN III palsy (down and out eye, dilated pupil, ptosis) + Contralateral spastic hemiplegia.

Diagram Labels: Key Structures Shown: oculomotor nerve (CN III) • cerebral peduncle (corticospinal tract) • red nucleus • tremor/ataxia • recurrent artery of Heubner (ACA) • Charcot's lenticulostriate artery (MCA)

question: Benedikt syndrome involves the midbrain tegmentum and injures CN III, the medial lemniscus, and the {{c1::red nucleus}}, presenting with ipsilateral CN III palsy and contralateral {{c2::tremor/ataxia}}.
answer:
Weber vs Benedikt vs Parinaud:
- Weber: CN III + Basis pedunculi (hemiplegia).
- Benedikt: CN III + Red nucleus + Substantia nigra (chorea/tremor).
- Parinaud: Dorsal midbrain tectum/pinealoma (upward gaze palsy, pseudo-Argyll Robertson pupil).

Diagram Labels: Key Structures Shown: oculomotor nerve (CN III) • cerebral peduncle (corticospinal tract) • red nucleus • tremor/ataxia • recurrent artery of Heubner (ACA) • Charcot's lenticulostriate artery (MCA)

question: The internal capsule blood supply: The anterior limb is supplied by {{c1::recurrent artery of Heubner (ACA)}}, the genu by ICA branches, and the posterior limb by {{c2::Charcot's lenticulostriate artery (MCA)}}.
answer:
Charcot's Artery of Cerebral Hemorrhage: Lateral lenticulostriate branches of MCA; most common site of hypertensive intracranial hemorrhage.

Diagram Labels: Key Structures Shown: oculomotor nerve (CN III) • cerebral peduncle (corticospinal tract) • red nucleus • tremor/ataxia • recurrent artery of Heubner (ACA) • Charcot's lenticulostriate artery (MCA)

question: The primary auditory cortex is located in Brodmann area {{c1::41 and 42}} (transverse temporal gyri of Heschl) on the superior temporal gyrus.
answer:
Key Cortical Areas:
- Area 4: Primary motor.
- Area 3, 1, 2: Primary sensory.
- Area 17: Primary visual (calcarine sulcus).
- Area 44, 45: Broca's motor speech (inferior frontal gyrus).
- Area 22: Wernicke's receptive language (superior temporal gyrus).

Diagram Labels: Key Structures Shown: oculomotor nerve (CN III) • cerebral peduncle (corticospinal tract) • red nucleus • tremor/ataxia • recurrent artery of Heubner (ACA) • Charcot's lenticulostriate artery (MCA)

question: Extradural (epidural) hemorrhage is classically caused by injury to the {c1::anterior division of the middle meningeal artery}.
answer: Pterion fracture is the most common site of injury. It presents as a lucid interval followed by rapid neurological deterioration.

question: Subdural hemorrhage is typically caused by the rupture or tearing of {c1::bridging veins}.
answer: Seen commonly in elderly patients and alcoholics due to cerebral atrophy stretching the bridging veins as they cross into the superior sagittal sinus.

question: A berry aneurysm of the anterior communicating artery is located close to the ACA and characteristically affects cranial nerve {c1::CN II (Optic nerve/chiasm)}, causing visual field defects.
answer: Anterior communicating artery (ACoA) aneurysms are the most common site of intracranial berry aneurysms and can present with bitemporal hemianopia.

question: A berry aneurysm of the posterior communicating artery is located close to the PCA and typically affects cranial nerve {c1::CN III (Oculomotor nerve)}, presenting with a blown pupil and ptosis.
answer: PCoA aneurysms classically present with painful oculomotor nerve palsy sparing parasympathetic fibers initially, but progressing to pupillary dilation.

question: Intracerebral hemorrhage (Charcot-Bouchard microaneurysms) commonly affects the lenticulostriate branches arising from the {c1::Charcot's artery / Middle Cerebral Artery}.
answer: Most commonly associated with chronic hypertension, frequently leading to damage in the basal ganglia (putamen/internal capsule).

question: The highest center for micturition and defecation is located in the {c1::paracentral lobule} supplied by the {c2::anterior cerebral artery (ACA)}.
answer:
Infarction of the ACA leads to contralateral lower limb weakness and urinary incontinence due to paracentral lobule involvement.

Diagram Labels: Key Structures Shown: paracentral lobule • anterior cerebral artery (ACA) • Posterior Cerebral Artery (PCA) • hemianopia

question: Broca's area (Brodmann areas 44, 45) and Wernicke's area (Brodmann areas 22, 39, 40) are supplied by the {c1::Middle Cerebral Artery (MCA)}.
answer:
Occlusion of the MCA leads to global aphasia, contralateral hemiplegia (face and arm > leg), and contralateral hemisensory loss.

Diagram Labels: Key Structures Shown: Middle Cerebral Artery (MCA)

question: The visual cortex is supplied by the {c1::Posterior Cerebral Artery (PCA)}, and its infarction classically leads to contralateral {c2::hemianopia} with macular sparing.
answer:
PCA also supplies the inferior surface of the temporal and occipital lobes.

Diagram Labels: Key Structures Shown: paracentral lobule • anterior cerebral artery (ACA) • Posterior Cerebral Artery (PCA) • hemianopia

question: The anterior thalamic nucleus receives input from the {c1::mammillary body} via the mammillothalamic tract as part of the {c2::Papez circuit}.
answer:
Involved in emotion, memory, and limbic system processing.

Diagram Labels: Key Structures Shown: mammillary body • Papez circuit • limbs and trunk • mouth and face • cerebellum, red nucleus, and globus pallidus

question: The Ventroposterolateral (VPL) nucleus of the thalamus relays sensations from the {c1::limbs and trunk}, while the Ventroposteromedial (VPM) nucleus relays sensations from the {c2::mouth and face} (including taste).
answer:
VPL receives the medial and spinal lemnisci; VPM receives the trigeminal lemniscus and gustatory pathways.

Diagram Labels: Key Structures Shown: mammillary body • Papez circuit • limbs and trunk • mouth and face • cerebellum, red nucleus, and globus pallidus

question: The Ventroanterior (VA) and Ventrolateral (VL) nuclei of the thalamus receive fibers from the {c1::cerebellum, red nucleus, and globus pallidus} and project to the motor and premotor cortices.
answer:
Critical relay for the extrapyramidal and motor coordination pathways.

Diagram Labels: Key Structures Shown: mammillary body • Papez circuit • limbs and trunk • mouth and face • cerebellum, red nucleus, and globus pallidus

question: The clavicle is the only long bone that ossifies in {{c1::membrane}}, is placed horizontally, and has {{c2::two}} primary ossification centers.
answer:
Clavicle Fractures: Most common fracture site is the junction of medial two-thirds and lateral one-third (weakest point). Medial fragment elevated by sternocleidomastoid, lateral pulled down by weight of arm and pectoralis major.

Diagram Labels: Key Structures Shown: membrane • two • atavistic • short head of biceps • greater tubercle • lesser tubercle

question: The Coracoid process of the scapula is an example of an {{c1::atavistic}} epiphysis and gives attachment to pectoralis minor, coracobrachialis, and {{c2::short head of biceps}}.
answer:
Epiphysis Types:
- Pressure: Head of femur, head of humerus.
- Traction: Greater/lesser trochanters, tubercles of humerus.
- Atavistic: Coracoid process, os trigonum.
- Aberrant: Head of 1st metacarpal, base of other metacarpals.

Diagram Labels: Key Structures Shown: membrane • two • atavistic • short head of biceps • greater tubercle • lesser tubercle

question: The rotator cuff consists of 4 muscles (SITS): Supraspinatus, Infraspinatus, and Teres minor inserting on the {{c1::greater tubercle}}, and Subscapularis inserting on the {{c2::lesser tubercle}}.
answer:
Rotator Cuff Functions & Nerves:
- Supraspinatus: Abduction (0-15°) - Suprascapular N.
- Infraspinatus: Lateral rotation - Suprascapular N.
- Teres minor: Lateral rotation - Axillary N.
- Subscapularis: Medial rotation - Upper & lower subscapular N.

Diagram Labels: Key Structures Shown: membrane • two • atavistic • short head of biceps • greater tubercle • lesser tubercle

question: The most commonly injured tendon in rotator cuff tear and subacromial impingement is the {{c1::supraspinatus}} tendon.
answer:
Painful Arc Syndrome: Pain between 60° to 120° of abduction due to supraspinatus tendon impingement under coracoacromial arch. Drop Arm test is positive.

Diagram Labels: Key Structures Shown: membrane • two • atavistic • short head of biceps • greater tubercle • lesser tubercle

question: Shoulder joint abduction stages: 0-15° is initiated by {{c1::supraspinatus}}, 15-90° by {{c2::deltoid}}, and 90-180° (overhead) by {{c3::serratus anterior and trapezius}}.
answer:
High Yield PYQ: Winging of scapula due to Long Thoracic Nerve (C5, C6, C7) palsy paralyzes Serratus Anterior, leading to inability to abduct arm above 90°.

Diagram Labels: Key Structures Shown: membrane • two • atavistic • short head of biceps • greater tubercle • lesser tubercle

question: Humeral fracture sites and injured nerves: Surgical neck injures {{c1::Axillary N.}}, Mid-shaft (spiral groove) injures {{c2::Radial N.}}, Supracondylar injures {{c3::Median N. (AIN)}}, and Medial epicondyle injures {{c4::Ulnar N.}}.
answer:
Mnemonic: A Rapid Medical Undergraduate (Axillary, Radial, Median, Ulnar from proximal to distal).

Diagram Labels: Key Structures Shown: membrane • two • atavistic • short head of biceps • greater tubercle • lesser tubercle

question: The quadrangular space transmits the {{c1::axillary nerve}} and the {{c2::posterior circumflex humeral artery}}.
answer:
Quadrangular Space Boundaries:
- Superior: Subscapularis / Teres minor.
- Inferior: Teres major.
- Medial: Long head of triceps.
- Lateral: Surgical neck of humerus.

Diagram Labels: Key Structures Shown: axillary nerve • posterior circumflex humeral artery • radial nerve • profunda brachii artery

question: The lower triangular space transmits the {{c1::radial nerve}} and {{c2::profunda brachii artery}} as they enter the spiral groove.
answer:
Upper Triangular Space: Transmits the circumflex scapular artery (branch of subscapular artery for scapular anastomosis).

Diagram Labels: Key Structures Shown: axillary nerve • posterior circumflex humeral artery • radial nerve • profunda brachii artery

question: The bicipital groove of the humerus provides insertion to three muscles described by 'Lady between two majors': {{c1::Latissimus dorsi}} on the floor, Pectoralis major on the lateral lip, and Teres major on the medial lip.
answer:
Contents of Bicipital Groove: Long head of biceps brachii tendon enveloped in synovial sheath, and ascending branch of anterior circumflex humeral artery.

Diagram Labels: Key Structures Shown: Latissimus dorsi

question: In Erb's palsy (injury to upper trunk C5-C6), the characteristic limb posture is {{c1::Waiter's tip / Policeman's tip position}} due to adduction, medial rotation of arm, and extension/pronation of forearm.
answer:
Klumpke's Palsy (C8-T1 lower trunk): Claw hand deformity (intrinsic hand muscles) + Ipsilateral Horner's syndrome (T1 sympathetic fibers).

Diagram Labels: Key Structures Shown: Waiter's tip / Policeman's tip position

question: The total number of intrinsic muscles in the hand is {c1::20}.
answer:
Intrinsic hand muscles include thenar, hypothenar, lumbricals, and interossei muscles.

Diagram Labels: Key Structures Shown: 20 • Flexor digitorum profundus (FDP) • Extensor digitorum tendon (Dorsal digital expansion)

question: The adductor pollicis muscle has its origin from the {c1::shaft of 3rd metacarpal}.
answer:
Adductor pollicis is also known as the 'Graveyard of ulnar N.' because the deep branch of the ulnar nerve passes right through it.

Diagram Labels: Key Structures Shown: shaft of 3rd metacarpal • proximal phalanx of thumb • Adductor pollicis (or note that AdP is separate/thenar group typically includes 3 main + adductor depending on classification, here listed with thenar/deep) • lateral aspect of the shaft of 1st MC

question: Adductor pollicis (AdP) inserts into the {c1::proximal phalanx of thumb}.
answer:
Acts to adduct the thumb. Supplied by the deep branch of the ulnar nerve.

Diagram Labels: Key Structures Shown: shaft of 3rd metacarpal • proximal phalanx of thumb • Adductor pollicis (or note that AdP is separate/thenar group typically includes 3 main + adductor depending on classification, here listed with thenar/deep) • lateral aspect of the shaft of 1st MC

question: The thenar muscles include Flexor pollicis brevis (FPB), Abductor pollicis brevis (AbPB), Opponens pollicis, and {c1::Adductor pollicis (or note that AdP is separate/thenar group typically includes 3 main + adductor depending on classification, here listed with thenar/deep)}. Specifically, Opponens pollicis inserts into the {c2::lateral aspect of the shaft of 1st MC}.
answer:
Most thenar muscles are supplied by the recurrent branch of the median nerve (except deep head of FPB sometimes by ulnar nerve).

Diagram Labels: Key Structures Shown: shaft of 3rd metacarpal • proximal phalanx of thumb • Adductor pollicis (or note that AdP is separate/thenar group typically includes 3 main + adductor depending on classification, here listed with thenar/deep) • lateral aspect of the shaft of 1st MC

question: In ulnar nerve injury, weakness of the adductor pollicis is compensated by flexion of the thumb using the flexor pollicis longus, a clinical finding known as {c1::Froment’s sign} (tested via the {c2::Book test}).
answer:
Froment's sign is positive when the patient flexes the interphalangeal joint of the thumb due to lack of adductor pollicis when trying to hold a paper/book between thumb and index finger.

Diagram Labels: Key Structures Shown: Froment’s sign • Book test

question: The subcutaneous muscle in the hypothenar eminence is the {c1::Palmaris brevis}, which is supplied by the {c2::superficial branch of ulnar N}.
answer: Wrinkles the skin of the hypothenar eminence to improve grip.

question: The hypothenar muscles consist of Palmaris brevis, Abductor digiti minimi, Flexor digiti minimi, and {c1::Opponens digiti minimi}.
answer: All hypothenar muscles are supplied by the deep branch of the ulnar nerve, except Palmaris brevis which is supplied by the superficial branch.

question: The lumbricals originate from the tendons of the {c1::Flexor digitorum profundus (FDP)} and insert into the {c2::Extensor digitorum tendon (Dorsal digital expansion)}.
answer:
Action: Flexion at metacarpophalangeal (MCP) joints and Extension at interphalangeal (IP) joints.

Diagram Labels: Key Structures Shown: 20 • Flexor digitorum profundus (FDP) • Extensor digitorum tendon (Dorsal digital expansion)

question: The 1st and 2nd lumbricals are {c1::unipennate} and supplied by the {c2::median nerve}, while the 3rd and 4th lumbricals are {c3::bipennate} and supplied by the {c4::ulnar nerve}.
answer: Mnemonic: Lateral two = Median N., Medial two = Ulnar N.

question: Interossei muscle actions follow the mnemonic PAD and DAB, which stand for Palmar interossei = {c1::Adduction} and Dorsal interossei = {c2::Abduction}.
answer: Palmar interossei are unipennate and 4 in number; Dorsal interossei are bipennate and 4 in number. All are supplied by the ulnar nerve.

question: Regarding interossei relations to the fingers: The middle finger serves as the axis of abduction/adduction, meaning dorsal interossei are {c1::absent on the thumb and little finger} and palmar interossei are {c2::absent on the middle finger}.
answer: Tested clinically using the Card test and Egawa test (movement of the middle finger).

question: The contents of the Cubital Fossa from medial to lateral are: {{c1::Median nerve}}, Brachial artery, Biceps tendon, and Radial nerve (MBBR).
answer:
Cubital Fossa Boundaries:
- Superior: Imaginary line connecting medial and lateral epicondyles.
- Medial: Pronator teres.
- Lateral: Brachioradialis.
- Floor: Brachialis and Supinator.
- Roof: Bicipital aponeurosis and Median cubital vein.

Diagram Labels: Key Structures Shown: Median nerve • bicipital aponeurosis

question: The Median Cubital Vein connects the cephalic vein laterally to the basilic vein medially and is separated from the brachial artery by the {{c1::bicipital aponeurosis}}.
answer:
Clinical Importance: Preferred site for venipuncture. Bicipital aponeurosis protects the underlying brachial artery and median nerve during needle insertion.

Diagram Labels: Key Structures Shown: Median nerve • bicipital aponeurosis

question: All anterior compartment forearm flexor muscles are innervated by the Median nerve EXCEPT {{c1::Flexor Carpi Ulnaris}} and the medial half of {{c2::Flexor Digitorum Profundus}} (supplied by Ulnar N.).
answer:
Mnemonic: 1.5 muscles supplied by Ulnar nerve in anterior forearm (FCU + medial 1/2 of FDP). The other 6.5 muscles by Median/AIN.

Diagram Labels: Key Structures Shown: Flexor Carpi Ulnaris • Flexor Digitorum Profundus • lateral half of Flexor Digitorum Profundus • median • thenar eminence

question: The Anterior Interosseous Nerve (branch of Median nerve) supplies 2.5 deep muscles: Flexor Pollicis Longus, Pronator Quadratus, and the {{c1::lateral half of Flexor Digitorum Profundus}}.
answer:
Kiloh-Nevin Syndrome (AIN syndrome): Inability to make the 'OK' sign (pincer grasp) due to paralysis of FPL and FDP index finger -> forms a flat pinch instead.

Diagram Labels: Key Structures Shown: Flexor Carpi Ulnaris • Flexor Digitorum Profundus • lateral half of Flexor Digitorum Profundus • median • thenar eminence

question: The Carpal Tunnel contains {{c1::10}} structures: the Median nerve and 9 flexor tendons (4 FDS, 4 FDP, and 1 FPL).
answer:
Structures Outside Carpal Tunnel: Ulnar nerve and artery (pass through Guyon's canal), Palmaris longus tendon, and Palmar cutaneous branch of median nerve (spared in carpal tunnel syndrome).

Diagram Labels: Key Structures Shown: 10 • 3.5 • superficial

question: In Carpal Tunnel Syndrome, sensory loss involves the palmar aspect of the lateral {{c1::3.5}} fingers, but sensation over the thenar eminence is PRESERVED because its palmar cutaneous branch passes {{c2::superficial}} to the flexor retinaculum.
answer:
Diagnostic Tests:
- Phalen's test: 60 seconds of wrist flexion reproduces paresthesia.
- Tinel's sign: Percussion over carpal tunnel produces tingling.

Diagram Labels: Key Structures Shown: 10 • 3.5 • superficial

question: The Supinator muscle is pierced by the {{c1::deep branch of the radial nerve (Posterior Interosseous Nerve)}} as it passes into the extensor compartment.
answer:
Frohse's Arcade: Fibrous proximal border of superficial head of supinator; most common site of PIN entrapment (causes finger drop without wrist drop).

Diagram Labels: Key Structures Shown: deep branch of the radial nerve (Posterior Interosseous Nerve)

question: The Anatomical Snuffbox boundaries: Medially bounded by {{c1::Extensor Pollicis Longus (EPL)}}, and laterally by {{c2::Abductor Pollicis Longus (APL) and Extensor Pollicis Brevis (EPB)}}.
answer:
Floor & Contents: Floor formed by scaphoid and trapezium. Content is the Radial Artery (palpable against scaphoid). Tenderness here indicates scaphoid fracture.

Diagram Labels: Key Structures Shown: Extensor Pollicis Longus (EPL) • Abductor Pollicis Longus (APL) and Extensor Pollicis Brevis (EPB)

question: The most common carpal bone to fracture is the {{c1::scaphoid}} (risk of avascular necrosis of proximal pole), and the most common to dislocate is the {{c2::lunate}} (compresses median nerve in carpal tunnel).
answer:
Blood supply to Scaphoid: Enters distally from radial artery branches and flows retrogradely; hence proximal pole fractures often suffer AVN.

Diagram Labels: Key Structures Shown: scaphoid • lunate

question: The Pronator Teres syndrome compresses the {{c1::median}} nerve between its humeral and ulnar heads, differing from carpal tunnel syndrome by causing sensory loss over the {{c2::thenar eminence}}.
answer:
Key Distinction: Palmar cutaneous branch arises proximal to carpal tunnel but distal to pronator teres, so thenar eminence is numb in Pronator Teres syndrome but spared in Carpal Tunnel.

Diagram Labels: Key Structures Shown: Flexor Carpi Ulnaris • Flexor Digitorum Profundus • lateral half of Flexor Digitorum Profundus • median • thenar eminence

question: The lumbrical muscles: the 1st and 2nd (lateral two) are unipennate and supplied by the {{c1::Median nerve}}, while the 3rd and 4th (medial two) are bipennate and supplied by the {{c2::deep branch of Ulnar nerve}}.
answer:
Action of Lumbricals: Flexion at Metacarpophalangeal (MCP) joints and extension at Interphalangeal (IP) joints (intrinsic plus position).

Diagram Labels: Key Structures Shown: Median nerve • deep branch of Ulnar nerve • deep branch of Ulnar nerve (C8-T1) • Palmar interossei • Dorsal interossei

question: All Interossei muscles of the hand (4 Palmar and 4 Dorsal) are innervated by the {{c1::deep branch of Ulnar nerve (C8-T1)}}.
answer:
PAD and DAB:
- Palmar Interossei ADduct fingers (PAD).
- Dorsal Interossei ABduct fingers (DAB).
Both also assist lumbricals in MCP flexion and IP extension.

Diagram Labels: Key Structures Shown: Median nerve • deep branch of Ulnar nerve • deep branch of Ulnar nerve (C8-T1) • Palmar interossei • Dorsal interossei

question: Card test tests the {{c1::Palmar interossei}} (adduction), while Egawa test tests the {{c2::Dorsal interossei}} (abduction of middle finger).
answer:
Ulnar Nerve Tests:
- Card test: Palmar interossei (holding paper between extended fingers).
- Froment's sign: Tests Adductor Pollicis (paralyzed -> flexes IP of thumb via FPL).
- Book test: Positive Froment's sign.

Diagram Labels: Key Structures Shown: Median nerve • deep branch of Ulnar nerve • deep branch of Ulnar nerve (C8-T1) • Palmar interossei • Dorsal interossei

question: Froment's sign tests the {{c1::Adductor Pollicis}} muscle (supplied by deep branch of ulnar nerve); compensatory flexion of the thumb IP joint occurs via the {{c2::Flexor Pollicis Longus (AIN/Median N.)}}.
answer:
High Yield PYQ: When patient grips a sheet of paper, thumb IP joint flexes because FPL compensates for weak adductor pollicis.

Diagram Labels: Key Structures Shown: Adductor Pollicis • Flexor Pollicis Longus (AIN/Median N.) • more severe in low ulnar nerve injury • recurrent motor branch of the Median

question: The 'Ulnar Paradox' states that claw hand deformity is {{c1::more severe in low ulnar nerve injury}} (at wrist) than in high ulnar nerve injury (at elbow).
answer:
Mechanism: In high lesion (at elbow), medial half of FDP is also paralyzed, reducing flexion pull on distal IP joints. In low lesion (at wrist), FDP is intact and exerts unopposed flexion pull on DIPs, making clawing much worse.

Diagram Labels: Key Structures Shown: Adductor Pollicis • Flexor Pollicis Longus (AIN/Median N.) • more severe in low ulnar nerve injury • recurrent motor branch of the Median

question: Benediction sign (Bishop's blessing / hand of benediction) occurs upon attempting to make a fist following a high {{c1::Median}} nerve injury.
answer:
Benediction vs Claw Hand:
- Benediction hand: Appears on active fist-making in Median nerve injury (cannot flex digits 1, 2, 3).
- Claw hand: Appears at rest in Ulnar nerve injury (hyperextension of MCP and flexion of IP joints of digits 4 and 5).

Diagram Labels: Key Structures Shown: Median • Ulnar • radial and ulnar • Superficial branch of Radial nerve • Median nerve

question: The Superficial Palmar Arch is formed primarily as the direct continuation of the {{c1::Ulnar}} artery and is completed by the superficial palmar branch of the radial artery.
answer:
Deep Palmar Arch: Formed primarily by the Radial artery entering the palm between the two heads of 1st dorsal interosseous, completed by deep branch of ulnar artery.

Diagram Labels: Key Structures Shown: Median • Ulnar • radial and ulnar • Superficial branch of Radial nerve • Median nerve

question: Allen's test evaluates the patency of the {{c1::radial and ulnar}} arterial arches before radial artery cannulation or blood gas sampling.
answer:
Procedure: Compress both arteries at wrist, patient clenches fist until blanched, release ulnar artery. Normal color return within 5-7 seconds indicates intact collateral flow via ulnar artery.

Diagram Labels: Key Structures Shown: Median • Ulnar • radial and ulnar • Superficial branch of Radial nerve • Median nerve

question: Ape-thumb deformity (flattening of thenar eminence and loss of thumb opposition) is caused by injury to the {{c1::recurrent motor branch of the Median}} nerve.
answer:
Thenar Muscles (OAF): Opponens pollicis, Abductor pollicis brevis, Flexor pollicis brevis (superficial head). All supplied by recurrent branch of median nerve (million dollar nerve).

Diagram Labels: Key Structures Shown: Adductor Pollicis • Flexor Pollicis Longus (AIN/Median N.) • more severe in low ulnar nerve injury • recurrent motor branch of the Median

question: The cutaneous innervation of the dorsum of the hand: the lateral 3.5 digits (up to proximal interphalangeal joints) is supplied by the {{c1::Superficial branch of Radial nerve}}, while the nail beds are supplied by the {{c2::Median nerve}}.
answer:
Nail Bed Innervation: Palmar branches of Median nerve curve dorsally to supply nail beds of lateral 3.5 fingers. Ulnar nerve supplies medial 1.5 fingers dorsal and palmar.

Diagram Labels: Key Structures Shown: Median • Ulnar • radial and ulnar • Superficial branch of Radial nerve • Median nerve

question: The ulnar nerve arises from the nerve roots {c1::C7-T1}.
answer:
High yield: The ulnar nerve is known as the musician's nerve because it controls the fine movements of the intrinsic hand muscles.

Diagram Labels: Key Structures Shown: C7-T1 • Flexor carpi ulnaris (FCU) • Guyon's canal • more prominent • 1st and 2nd lumbricals

question: The ulnar nerve passes through the cubital tunnel, which is the space between the two heads of the {c1::Flexor carpi ulnaris (FCU)}.
answer:
Cubital tunnel syndrome causes numbness and tingling in the ring and little fingers.

Diagram Labels: Key Structures Shown: C7-T1 • Flexor carpi ulnaris (FCU) • Guyon's canal • more prominent • 1st and 2nd lumbricals

question: At the wrist, the ulnar nerve passes through {c1::Guyon's canal} along with the ulnar artery.
answer:
Compression in Guyon's canal can occur in cyclists (cyclist's palsy) leading to weakness of hypothenar and interossei muscles.

Diagram Labels: Key Structures Shown: C7-T1 • Flexor carpi ulnaris (FCU) • Guyon's canal • more prominent • 1st and 2nd lumbricals

question: In a lower ulnar nerve injury (at the wrist), the ulnar claw hand is {c1::more prominent} because the Flexor digitorum profundus (FDP) is spared, resulting in greater flexion of the ring and little fingers.
answer:
Higher injury affects FDP resulting in less flexion (less prominent claw/ulnar paradox).

Diagram Labels: Key Structures Shown: C7-T1 • Flexor carpi ulnaris (FCU) • Guyon's canal • more prominent • 1st and 2nd lumbricals

question: In an ulnar nerve injury, the intrinsic muscles of the hand are affected except the {c1::1st and 2nd lumbricals}, which are supplied by the median nerve.
answer:
Loss of interossei and 3rd/4th lumbricals leads to the characteristic ulnar claw hand deformity.

Diagram Labels: Key Structures Shown: C7-T1 • Flexor carpi ulnaris (FCU) • Guyon's canal • more prominent • 1st and 2nd lumbricals

question: The Femoral Triangle contents from lateral to medial are: {{c1::Femoral nerve}}, Femoral artery, Femoral vein, and Deep inguinal lymph nodes (NAVeL).
answer:
Key Anatomical Fact: The Femoral Nerve lies OUTSIDE the femoral sheath, whereas the artery, vein, and canal lie INSIDE the femoral sheath.

Diagram Labels: Key Structures Shown: Femoral nerve • Inguinal ligament • Pectineal (Cooper's) ligament • Lacunar (Gimbernat's) ligament • Cloquet's or Rosenmüller's

question: The Femoral Ring is bounded anteriorly by the {{c1::Inguinal ligament}}, posteriorly by the {{c2::Pectineal (Cooper's) ligament}}, medially by the {{c3::Lacunar (Gimbernat's) ligament}}, and laterally by the femoral vein.
answer:
Femoral Hernia: Enters femoral canal via femoral ring, emerges below and lateral to pubic tubercle. More common in females due to wider pelvis.

Diagram Labels: Key Structures Shown: Femoral nerve • Inguinal ligament • Pectineal (Cooper's) ligament • Lacunar (Gimbernat's) ligament • Cloquet's or Rosenmüller's

question: The deep inguinal lymph node located inside the femoral canal is known as the {{c1::Cloquet's or Rosenmüller's}} node.
answer:
Clinical Significance: Drains glans penis/clitoris and deep perineal structures. Enlargement may mimic an incarcerated femoral hernia.

Diagram Labels: Key Structures Shown: Femoral nerve • Inguinal ligament • Pectineal (Cooper's) ligament • Lacunar (Gimbernat's) ligament • Cloquet's or Rosenmüller's

question: The femoral sheath is formed anteriorly by the {{c1::fascia transversalis}} and posteriorly by the {{c2::fascia iliaca}}.
answer:
Compartments of Femoral Sheath:
- Lateral: Femoral artery + femoral branch of genitofemoral nerve.
- Intermediate: Femoral vein.
- Medial (Femoral canal): Lymphatics and Cloquet's node.

Diagram Labels: Key Structures Shown: fascia transversalis • fascia iliaca

question: The Obturator nerve (L2, L3, L4) exits the pelvis through the obturator canal and divides into anterior and posterior branches separated by the {{c1::Adductor Brevis}} muscle.
answer:
Referred Pain: Howship-Romberg sign in obturator hernia: pain radiating along medial thigh to knee due to compression of obturator nerve (articular branch to hip and knee).

Diagram Labels: Key Structures Shown: Adductor Brevis

question: The Adductor Canal (Hunter's canal) boundaries: Anteromedially bounded by the {{c1::Sartorius}}, laterally by {{c2::Vastus medialis}}, and posteriorly by Adductor longus and Adductor magnus.
answer:
Contents of Hunter's Canal: Femoral artery, Femoral vein (passes posterior to artery), Saphenous nerve, and Nerve to vastus medialis.

Diagram Labels: Key Structures Shown: Sartorius • Vastus medialis • Saphenous nerve • Tibial branch of Sciatic nerve • Obturator nerve (posterior division)

question: The structure that exits the adductor canal by piercing the anterior wall (subsartorial fascia) with the saphenous branch of descending genicular artery is the {{c1::Saphenous nerve}}.
answer:
Course: Accompanies great saphenous vein down the medial leg; injury during varicose vein stripping causes numbness over medial leg and medial border of foot.

Diagram Labels: Key Structures Shown: Sartorius • Vastus medialis • Saphenous nerve • Tibial branch of Sciatic nerve • Obturator nerve (posterior division)

question: The Great Saphenous Vein originates from the medial end of the dorsal venous arch, ascends anterior to the {{c1::medial malleolus}}, and drains into the femoral vein at the saphenous opening.
answer:
Saphenous Opening: Located 3.5 cm inferolateral to pubic tubercle; covered by cribriform fascia. Cutdown performed 1-2 cm anterior to medial malleolus.

Diagram Labels: Key Structures Shown: medial malleolus • Pes Anserinus (goose foot)

question: The Adductor Magnus has dual innervation: the adductor (hamstring) part is innervated by the {{c1::Tibial branch of Sciatic nerve}}, and the pubic (adductor) part by the {{c2::Obturator nerve (posterior division)}}.
answer:
Adductor Hiatus: Opening in adductor magnus tendon through which femoral vessels enter the popliteal fossa as popliteal vessels.

Diagram Labels: Key Structures Shown: Sartorius • Vastus medialis • Saphenous nerve • Tibial branch of Sciatic nerve • Obturator nerve (posterior division)

question: The Sartorius, Gracilis, and Semitendinosus insert into the upper medial surface of the tibia to form the {{c1::Pes Anserinus (goose foot)}}.
answer:
Mnemonic: 'Say Grace before Tea' (Sartorius - Femoral N., Gracilis - Obturator N., Semitendinosus - Sciatic N.). Pes anserine bursitis causes medial knee pain.

Diagram Labels: Key Structures Shown: medial malleolus • Pes Anserinus (goose foot)

question: The gluteus maximus muscle originates from the posterior surface of the sacrum and inserts into the {c1::gluteal tuberosity}.
answer: Gluteus maximus acts as a powerful external rotator and extensor at the hip joint.

question: The anterior superior iliac spine (ASIS) serves as the attachment site for the inguinal ligament and the {c1::sartorius} muscle.
answer:
ASIS is a crucial palpable bony landmark in the pelvis. Sartorius and tensor fascia lata originate here.

Diagram Labels: Key Structures Shown: sartorius • anterior inferior iliac spine (AIIS) • lesser trochanter • hamstring • coccygeal

question: The straight head of the rectus femoris muscle originates from the {c1::anterior inferior iliac spine (AIIS)}.
answer:
Rectus femoris is an anterior compartment muscle responsible for flexion at the hip joint and extension at the knee joint.

Diagram Labels: Key Structures Shown: sartorius • anterior inferior iliac spine (AIIS) • lesser trochanter • hamstring • coccygeal

question: The iliopsoas muscle inserts into the {c1::lesser trochanter} of the femur, producing flexion at the hip joint.
answer:
Iliopsoas is the primary flexor of the thigh at the hip joint.

Diagram Labels: Key Structures Shown: sartorius • anterior inferior iliac spine (AIIS) • lesser trochanter • hamstring • coccygeal

question: The ischial tuberosity provides weight-bearing support for the hip and serves as the origin point for the {c1::hamstring} muscles.
answer:
Hamstring muscles include semitendinosus, semimembranosus, and long head of biceps femoris.

Diagram Labels: Key Structures Shown: sartorius • anterior inferior iliac spine (AIIS) • lesser trochanter • hamstring • coccygeal

question: The ischial spine is located at the level of the {c1::coccygeal} vertebrae.
answer:
It separates the greater sciatic notch (GSN) from the lesser sciatic notch (LSN).

Diagram Labels: Key Structures Shown: sartorius • anterior inferior iliac spine (AIIS) • lesser trochanter • hamstring • coccygeal

question: The iliotibial band (ITB) is a thickened modification of the {c1::fascia lata} (deep fascia of the thigh).
answer:
It originates from the iliac bone and inserts into the lateral tibial condyle (Gerdy's tubercle).

Diagram Labels: Key Structures Shown: fascia lata • gluteus maximus (GM)

question: The two primary muscles that insert into the iliotibial band are the tensor fascia lata (TFL) and the {c1::gluteus maximus (GM)}.
answer:
ITB contracture leads to abnormal biomechanics and knee pain (Iliotibial Band Syndrome).

Diagram Labels: Key Structures Shown: fascia lata • gluteus maximus (GM)

question: The pudendal nerve arises from nerve roots {c1::S2-S4} and supplies the muscles of the perineum and internal pudendal vessels.
answer: Nerve injury to the pudendal nerve results in loss of voluntary control of sphincters (incontinence).

question: At the hip joint, the FABER movement stands for Flexion, Abduction, and {c1::External rotation}.
answer: Useful clinical test for hip pathology and sacroiliac joint dysfunction.

question: The Popliteal Fossa contents from superficial to deep are: {{c1::Tibial nerve}}, Popliteal vein, and Popliteal artery.
answer:
Popliteal Artery: Deepest structure, closest to the femur floor and capsule; vulnerable to tear in supracondylar fracture of femur or posterior knee dislocation.

Diagram Labels: Key Structures Shown: Tibial nerve • laterally rotating the femur on the fixed tibia

question: The Common Peroneal (Fibular) Nerve winds around the {{c1::neck of the fibula}}, where it is highly vulnerable to fracture or compression, causing {{c2::foot drop and loss of sensation over dorsum of foot}}.
answer:
Clinical Triad of Foot Drop:
1. Loss of dorsiflexion (Tibialis Anterior - Deep Peroneal N.).
2. Loss of eversion (Peroneus Longus/Brevis - Superficial Peroneal N.).
3. High-steppage gait.

Diagram Labels: Key Structures Shown: neck of the fibula • foot drop and loss of sensation over dorsum of foot • Deep Peroneal (Fibular)

question: The Tarsal Tunnel is covered by the flexor retinaculum behind the medial malleolus and transmits (from anterior to posterior): {{c1::Tibialis posterior, Flexor digitorum longus, Posterior tibial artery, Tibial nerve, Flexor hallucis longus}} (Tom, Dick And Very Nervous Harry).
answer:
Tarsal Tunnel Syndrome: Compression of posterior tibial nerve behind medial malleolus causes burning pain and paresthesia over the sole of the foot.

Diagram Labels: Key Structures Shown: Tibialis posterior, Flexor digitorum longus, Posterior tibial artery, Tibial nerve, Flexor hallucis longus

question: The most commonly injured ligament in an inversion sprain of the ankle is the {{c1::Anterior Talofibular Ligament (ATFL)}}.
answer:
Lateral Ankle Ligaments:
1. Anterior Talofibular (weakest, most common tear).
2. Calcaneofibular.
3. Posterior Talofibular (strongest).

Diagram Labels: Key Structures Shown: Anterior Talofibular Ligament (ATFL) • talus • sustentaculum tali and navicular

question: The Deltoid ligament (medial collateral ligament of ankle) attaches superiorly to the medial malleolus and has a deep part attaching to the {{c1::talus}} and superficial part attaching to the {{c2::sustentaculum tali and navicular}}.
answer:
Spring Ligament (Plantar Calcaneonavicular): Supports the head of the talus and maintains the medial longitudinal arch. Deltoid ligament blends with it.

Diagram Labels: Key Structures Shown: Anterior Talofibular Ligament (ATFL) • talus • sustentaculum tali and navicular

question: The keystone of the medial longitudinal arch of the foot is the {{c1::talus (head)}}, while the keystone of the lateral longitudinal arch is the {{c2::cuboid}}.
answer:
Arches of Foot:
- Medial arch: Higher, dynamic (shock absorber). Maintained by Tibialis posterior, FHL, FDL, plantar fascia, and spring ligament.
- Lateral arch: Lower, static (weight transmission). Maintained by long and short plantar ligaments.

Diagram Labels: Key Structures Shown: talus (head) • cuboid

question: The Popliteus muscle unlocks the knee joint during the beginning of flexion by {{c1::laterally rotating the femur on the fixed tibia}} (or medially rotating the tibia on the femur).
answer:
Locking vs Unlocking:
- Locking: Medial rotation of femur on tibia during terminal extension (passive, by ACL).
- Unlocking: Lateral rotation of femur by Popliteus (Nerve to popliteus/Tibial N.).

Diagram Labels: Key Structures Shown: Tibial nerve • laterally rotating the femur on the fixed tibia

question: The Anterior Cruciate Ligament (ACL) prevents {{c1::anterior displacement of the tibia on the femur}} and hyperextension of the knee.
answer:
Tests for Cruciate Ligaments:
- ACL: Lachman test (most sensitive), Anterior drawer test, Pivot-shift test.
- PCL: Posterior drawer test, Posterior sag sign.

Diagram Labels: Key Structures Shown: anterior displacement of the tibia on the femur • Anterior Cruciate Ligament (ACL) • Medial Collateral Ligament (MCL) • Medial Meniscus

question: The 'Unhappy Triad' of O'Donoghue classically involves simultaneous rupture of the {{c1::Anterior Cruciate Ligament (ACL)}}, {{c2::Medial Collateral Ligament (MCL)}}, and {{c3::Medial Meniscus}} (though lateral meniscus is more frequently torn acutely).
answer:
Mechanism: Lateral blow to knee while foot is planted (valgus stress, flexion, and external rotation).

Diagram Labels: Key Structures Shown: anterior displacement of the tibia on the femur • Anterior Cruciate Ligament (ACL) • Medial Collateral Ligament (MCL) • Medial Meniscus

question: The sensory supply to the first web space on the dorsum of the foot is provided by the {{c1::Deep Peroneal (Fibular)}} nerve.
answer:
Sensory Branches of Peroneal N.:
- Deep Peroneal: Skin of 1st web space only.
- Superficial Peroneal: Rest of dorsum of foot and toes (except lateral border of little toe - Sural N., and medial border - Saphenous N.).

Diagram Labels: Key Structures Shown: neck of the fibula • foot drop and loss of sensation over dorsum of foot • Deep Peroneal (Fibular)

question: The Lisfranc ligament extends from the medial cuneiform to the base of the {c1::2nd metatarsal}.
answer:
Injury to the Lisfranc ligament leads to an increased gap between the 1st and 2nd metatarsals, highly tested in midfoot trauma and sports injuries.

Diagram Labels: Key Structures Shown: 2nd metatarsal • plantar calcaneonavicular ligament • lateral longitudinal arch

question: The spring ligament is also known anatomically as the {c1::plantar calcaneonavicular ligament}.
answer:
It runs from the navicular tuberosity to the calcaneum, supporting the head of the talus. Injury or laxity results in flat foot (pes planus) due to loss of support for the medial longitudinal arch.

Diagram Labels: Key Structures Shown: 2nd metatarsal • plantar calcaneonavicular ligament • lateral longitudinal arch

question: The long and short plantar calcaneocuboid ligaments provide primary structural support for the {c1::lateral longitudinal arch} of the foot.
answer:
Crucial for maintaining foot biomechanics and shock absorption during bipedal gait.

Diagram Labels: Key Structures Shown: 2nd metatarsal • plantar calcaneonavicular ligament • lateral longitudinal arch

question: During a severe eversion injury of the ankle, the medial ligament ({c1::deltoid ligament}) is typically injured, while laterally it is common to see a fracture of the {c2::lateral malleolus}.
answer:
The deltoid ligament is a strong triangular ligament preventing excessive eversion.

Diagram Labels: Key Structures Shown: deltoid ligament • lateral malleolus

question: The most commonly injured ligament in an inversion injury of the ankle is the {c1::anterior talofibular ligament}, especially when the foot is in a {c2::plantar-flexed} position.
answer:
Inversion injuries also involve the calcaneofibular and posterior talofibular ligaments in more severe grades.

Diagram Labels: Key Structures Shown: anterior talofibular ligament • plantar-flexed

question: The root value of the sciatic nerve is {c1::L4, L5, S1, S2, S3}.
answer: It exits the greater sciatic notch deep to the piriformis muscle and gives no muscular branches in the gluteal region.

question: In the popliteal fossa, the sciatic nerve typically divides into its two main components: the tibial nerve and the {c1::common peroneal nerve (CPN)}.
answer: The common peroneal nerve wraps around the neck of the fibula, making it extremely vulnerable to external compression and fractures.

question: Tibial nerve injury leads to paralysis of plantar flexors and intrinsic foot muscles, resulting in a {c1::calcaneovalgus} deformity and a {c2::calcaneal (heel) gait}.
answer: Patients with a calcaneal gait walk primarily on their heels because they cannot plantarflex.

question: Common peroneal nerve (CPN) injury most commonly occurs at the {c1::neck of the fibula}, resulting in foot drop, an {c2::equinovarus} deformity, and a high steppage gait.
answer: Affected muscles include dorsiflexors (Tibialis anterior) and evertors (Peroneus longus and brevis).

question: The superficial peroneal nerve (SPN) supplies the {c1::lateral compartment} of the leg containing the evertors, whereas the deep peroneal nerve (DPN) supplies the {c2::anterior compartment} containing the dorsiflexors.
answer: DPN also supplies cutaneous sensation to the 1st web space of the foot.

question: Major diaphragmatic openings and their vertebral levels: Vena Cava foramen is at {{c1::T8}}, Esophageal hiatus is at {{c2::T10}}, and Aortic hiatus is at {{c3::T12}}.
answer:
Mnemonic: 'Voice Of America' -> V=8 (Vena cava), O=10 (Esophagus), A=12 (Aorta). Numbers correspond to letters: T8 (8), T10 (10), T12 (12).

Diagram Labels: Key Structures Shown: T8 • T10 • T12 • vagal trunks • left gastric • thoracic duct

question: The Esophageal hiatus (T10) transmits the esophagus, the anterior and posterior {{c1::vagal trunks}}, and the esophageal branches of the {{c2::left gastric}} artery and vein.
answer:
Muscle of Origin: Esophageal hiatus is formed entirely by the right crus of the diaphragm looping around the esophagus (sling of right crus).

Diagram Labels: Key Structures Shown: T8 • T10 • T12 • vagal trunks • left gastric • thoracic duct

question: The Aortic hiatus (T12) transmits the abdominal aorta, the {{c1::thoracic duct}}, and the {{c2::azygos vein}}.
answer:
Boundaries: Located behind the median arcuate ligament between right and left crura; not affected by diaphragmatic contraction during breathing.

Diagram Labels: Key Structures Shown: T8 • T10 • T12 • vagal trunks • left gastric • thoracic duct

question: The sensory supply to the central tendon of the diaphragm is provided by the {{c1::Phrenic nerve (C3, C4, C5)}}, which explains referred pain to the {{c2::shoulder tip (C4 dermatome/supraclavicular nerve)}}.
answer:
Diaphragm Innervation:
- Motor: Solely by Phrenic nerve (C3-C5).
- Sensory: Central part by Phrenic N.; Peripheral part by lower 6 intercostal and subcostal nerves (referred to abdominal wall).

Diagram Labels: Key Structures Shown: T8 • T10 • T12 • vagal trunks • left gastric • thoracic duct

question: In the costal groove along the lower border of each rib, the intercostal neurovascular bundle is arranged from superior to inferior as: {{c1::Intercostal Vein, Intercostal Artery, Intercostal Nerve}} (VAN).
answer:
Thoracocentesis (Pleural Tap): Needle is inserted immediately above the upper border of the lower rib to avoid injuring the VAN bundle in the costal groove of the upper rib.

Diagram Labels: Key Structures Shown: Intercostal Vein, Intercostal Artery, Intercostal Nerve • T4-T5 • 2nd • L1-L2 • left internal jugular and left subclavian veins • first part of Subclavian artery

question: The Sternal Angle of Louis (manubriosternal joint) lies opposite the {{c1::T4-T5}} intervertebral disc and articulates with the {{c2::2nd}} costal cartilage.
answer:
Key Events at T4-T5 Level (RAT PLANT):
- Rib 2 articulates.
- Aortic arch begins and ends.
- Trachea bifurcates into primary bronchi.
- Pulmonary trunk bifurcates.
- Left recurrent laryngeal nerve hooks around arch.
- Azygos vein arches over right bronchus.
- Thoracic duct crosses from right to left.

Diagram Labels: Key Structures Shown: Intercostal Vein, Intercostal Artery, Intercostal Nerve • T4-T5 • 2nd • L1-L2 • left internal jugular and left subclavian veins • first part of Subclavian artery

question: The right lung has {{c1::3}} lobes and 10 bronchopulmonary segments, with {{c2::horizontal and oblique}} fissures, whereas the left lung has 2 lobes, 1 oblique fissure, and a lingula.
answer:

- Right lung: Eparterial bronchus (superior), Pulmonary artery, Hyparterial bronchus, Pulmonary veins (anterior/inferior).
- Left lung: Pulmonary artery (most superior), Principal bronchus, Pulmonary veins.

question: The most common bronchopulmonary segment for aspirated foreign bodies in the supine position is the {{c1::superior (apical) segment of the right lower lobe}}.
answer:
Aspiration Anatomy: Right main bronchus is wider, shorter (2.5 cm), and more vertical (25°) than left (5 cm, 45°); hence foreign bodies enter the right lung preferentially.

Diagram Labels: Key Structures Shown: 3 • horizontal and oblique • superior (apical) segment of the right lower lobe

question: The thoracic duct originates from the cisterna chyli at the level of {{c1::L1-L2}}, enters thorax through aortic hiatus, and drains into the junction of {{c2::left internal jugular and left subclavian veins}}.
answer:
Course & Tributaries: Ascends in posterior mediastinum between azygos vein (right) and aorta (left), crosses from right to left at T4-T5. Drains lymph from entire body except right upper quadrant.

Diagram Labels: Key Structures Shown: Intercostal Vein, Intercostal Artery, Intercostal Nerve • T4-T5 • 2nd • L1-L2 • left internal jugular and left subclavian veins • first part of Subclavian artery

question: The Internal Thoracic (Mammary) Artery arises from the {{c1::first part of Subclavian artery}} and terminates at the 6th intercostal space by dividing into the {{c2::Superior Epigastric and Musculophrenic}} arteries.
answer:
Clinical Use: Internal Mammary Artery (LIMA) is the graft of choice for Coronary Artery Bypass Grafting (CABG) to the Left Anterior Descending (LAD) artery.

question: The Transverse Pericardial Sinus lies posterior to the {{c1::ascending aorta and pulmonary trunk}} and anterior to the {{c2::superior vena cava and left atrium}}.
answer:
Surgical Significance: In cardiac surgery for cardiopulmonary bypass, a clamp or ligature is passed through the transverse sinus to temporarily stop systemic blood flow.

Diagram Labels: Key Structures Shown: ascending aorta and pulmonary trunk • superior vena cava and left atrium • left atrium

question: The Oblique Pericardial Sinus is a blind pocket behind the {{c1::left atrium}}, bounded by the pulmonary veins and inferior vena cava.
answer:
Clinical Note: Fluid can collect here in pericardial effusion. Left atrium enlargement (mitral stenosis) compresses the esophagus causing dysphagia.

question: In the right atrium, the crista terminalis internally separates the smooth posterior part (sinus venarum, derived from {{c1::sinus venosus}}) from the rough anterior part (atrium proper, derived from {{c2::primitive atrium}}).
answer:
SA Node Location: SA node lies in the upper part of the crista terminalis near the opening of the superior vena cava.

question: The Fossa Ovalis in the interatrial septum: the floor is derived from the {{c1::septum primum}}, and the prominent limbus (annulus ovalis) is derived from the {{c2::septum secundum}}.
answer:
Patent Foramen Ovale (PFO): Failure of fusion of septum primum and septum secundum; risk of paradoxical embolism (DVT causing stroke).

question: The AV node (Atrioventricular node) is located in the {{c1::Triangle of Koch}} in the right atrium.
answer:
Boundaries of Triangle of Koch:
1. Base: Coronary sinus orifice.
2. Superior: Tendon of Todaro.
3. Inferior: Septal leaflet of tricuspid valve.

Diagram Labels: Key Structures Shown: sinus venosus • primitive atrium • septum primum • septum secundum • Triangle of Koch • right branch of the bundle of His

question: The Moderator Band (septomarginal trabecula) in the right ventricle connects the interventricular septum to the anterior papillary muscle and carries the {{c1::right branch of the bundle of His}}.
answer:

Diagram Labels: Key Structures Shown: sinus venosus • primitive atrium • septum primum • septum secundum • Triangle of Koch • right branch of the bundle of His

question: The Left Anterior Descending (LAD) artery is a branch of the Left Coronary Artery and runs with the {{c1::Great Cardiac Vein}} in the anterior interventricular groove.
answer:
Most Common Occlusion: LAD is the most frequently occluded coronary artery in myocardial infarction ('widow maker'). Supplies anterior 2/3 of IV septum and anterior wall of LV.

question: The Posterior Interventricular Artery (Posterior Descending Artery - PDA) runs with the {{c1::Middle Cardiac Vein}} in the posterior interventricular sulcus.
answer:
Coronary Dominance: Determined by which artery gives origin to the PDA:
- Right dominant (85%): PDA from Right Coronary Artery.
- Left dominant (10%): PDA from Left Circumflex Artery.
- Codominant (5%): Both supply posterior septum.

question: The Sinoatrial (SA) node is supplied by the SA nodal artery, which arises from the {{c1::Right Coronary Artery}} in 60% of cases and from the {{c2::Left Circumflex Artery}} in 40%.
answer:
AV Node Blood Supply: Arises from RCA in 90% (crux of heart) and from LCx in 10%.

Diagram Labels: Key Structures Shown: Great Cardiac Vein • Middle Cardiac Vein • Right Coronary Artery • Left Circumflex Artery • right atrium • Thebesian

question: The Coronary Sinus is the largest vein draining the heart, empties directly into the {{c1::right atrium}}, and is guarded by the {{c2::Thebesian}} valve.
answer:
Embryological Origin: Left horn of the sinus venosus.
Main tributaries: Great cardiac vein, Middle cardiac vein, Small cardiac vein, Posterior vein of left ventricle.
