question: The oblique sinus of the pericardial cavity is a closed cul-de-sac located behind the {c1::left atrium} and bounded by the four pulmonary veins.
answer: High-yield point: The oblique sinus allows free expansion of the left atrium during ventricular systole without compressing the esophagus.

question: In the interior of the right atrium, the rough anterior wall is separated from the smooth posterior wall by a muscular ridge known as the {c1::crista terminalis}.
answer:
The crista terminalis marks the embryological junction between the sinus venosus (smooth posterior) and the primitive atrium (rough anterior with musculi pectinati).

Diagram Labels: Key Structures Shown: crista terminalis • coronary sinus

question: The Sinoatrial (SA) node is located in the right atrium near the upper end of the {c1::crista terminalis}, close to the opening of the superior vena cava.
answer:
Known as the natural pacemaker of the heart, supplied predominantly by the right coronary artery (RCA).

Diagram Labels: Key Structures Shown: crista terminalis • coronary sinus

question: The Triangle of Koch, which contains the Atrioventricular (AV) node, is bounded by the tendon of Todaro, the base of the septal cusp of the tricuspid valve, and the orifice of the {c1::coronary sinus}.
answer:
Crucial surgical landmark in electrophysiology and ablation procedures for supraventricular tachycardias.

Diagram Labels: Key Structures Shown: crista terminalis • coronary sinus

question: In the interior of the right ventricle, the rough inflowing part is separated from the smooth outflowing part (infundibulum) by the {c1::supraventricular crest}.
answer:
The infundibulum (conus arteriosus) leads up to the pulmonary trunk and is derived from the bulbus cordis.

Diagram Labels: Key Structures Shown: supraventricular crest

question: Cardiac dominance is determined by the origin of the {c1::posterior interventricular artery (PIVA)}.
answer:
If PIVA arises from the RCA, it is right dominance (most common, ~85%). If it arises from the circumflex artery, it is left dominance.

Diagram Labels: Key Structures Shown: posterior interventricular artery (PIVA) • Right Coronary Artery (RCA)

question: The blood supply to the Sinoatrial (SA) node, Atrioventricular (AV) node, and Bundle of His is predominantly provided by the {c1::Right Coronary Artery (RCA)}.
answer:
In contrast, the right and left bundle branches (RBB & LBB) are supplied by the Left Coronary Artery (LCA).

Diagram Labels: Key Structures Shown: posterior interventricular artery (PIVA) • Right Coronary Artery (RCA)

question: Unlike most cardiac veins, the {c1::anterior cardiac veins} do not drain into the coronary sinus; instead, they open directly into the right atrium.
answer:
They cross the atrioventricular groove and drain the anterior wall of the right ventricle directly.

Diagram Labels: Key Structures Shown: anterior cardiac veins • Left Anterior Descending (LAD) • posterior interventricular artery (PIVA)

question: The Great Cardiac Vein runs together and is accompanied in its course by the {c1::Left Anterior Descending (LAD)} artery and the circumflex artery.
answer:
It eventually dilates to form the coronary sinus in the posterior part of the coronary sulcus.

Diagram Labels: Key Structures Shown: anterior cardiac veins • Left Anterior Descending (LAD) • posterior interventricular artery (PIVA)

question: The Middle Cardiac Vein runs in the posterior interventricular sulcus and is directly accompanied by the {c1::posterior interventricular artery (PIVA)}.
answer:
It drains into the right-hand end of the coronary sinus.

Diagram Labels: Key Structures Shown: anterior cardiac veins • Left Anterior Descending (LAD) • posterior interventricular artery (PIVA)

question: The anterior wall of the inguinal canal is formed by the {c1::external oblique aponeurosis} and laterally by the {c2::internal oblique muscle}.
answer:
High-yield boundary detail: The internal oblique only contributes to the lateral 1/3rd of the anterior wall.

Diagram Labels: Key Structures Shown: external oblique aponeurosis • internal oblique muscle • fascia transversalis • conjoint tendon (falx inguinalis) • arching fibers of internal oblique and transversus abdominis • inguinal ligament

question: The posterior wall of the inguinal canal is formed by the {c1::fascia transversalis} and medially by the {c2::conjoint tendon (falx inguinalis)}.
answer:
Weakness in the posterior wall (specifically Hesselbach triangle) leads to direct inguinal hernias.

Diagram Labels: Key Structures Shown: external oblique aponeurosis • internal oblique muscle • fascia transversalis • conjoint tendon (falx inguinalis) • arching fibers of internal oblique and transversus abdominis • inguinal ligament

question: The roof of the inguinal canal is formed by the {c1::arching fibers of internal oblique and transversus abdominis}.
answer:
The roof arches over the contents of the inguinal canal from the deep to the superficial ring.

Diagram Labels: Key Structures Shown: external oblique aponeurosis • internal oblique muscle • fascia transversalis • conjoint tendon (falx inguinalis) • arching fibers of internal oblique and transversus abdominis • inguinal ligament

question: The floor of the inguinal canal is formed by the {c1::inguinal ligament} and medially by the {c2::lacunar ligament}.
answer:
The lacunar ligament (Gimbernat's ligament) forms the medial boundary of the femoral ring.

Diagram Labels: Key Structures Shown: external oblique aponeurosis • internal oblique muscle • fascia transversalis • conjoint tendon (falx inguinalis) • arching fibers of internal oblique and transversus abdominis • inguinal ligament

question: The deep inguinal ring is an opening in the {c1::fascia transversalis}, whereas the superficial inguinal ring is an opening in the {c2::external oblique aponeurosis}.
answer:
Crucial distinction tested frequently in NEET PG to differentiate layers of entry and exit.

Diagram Labels: Key Structures Shown: external oblique aponeurosis • internal oblique muscle • fascia transversalis • conjoint tendon (falx inguinalis) • arching fibers of internal oblique and transversus abdominis • inguinal ligament

question: The falciform ligament connects the liver to the {c1::anterior abdominal wall} and contains the {c2::ligamentum teres hepatis} in its free margin.
answer:
Ligamentum teres is the fibrous remnant of the embryonic left umbilical vein.

Diagram Labels: Key Structures Shown: anterior abdominal wall • ligamentum teres hepatis • splenic artery • tail of the pancreas • short gastric arteries • left gastroepiploic vessels

question: The splenorenal (lienorenal) ligament contains the {c1::splenic artery} and the {c2::tail of the pancreas}.
answer:
Surgeons must ligate vessels carefully here during splenectomy to avoid damaging the pancreatic tail.

Diagram Labels: Key Structures Shown: anterior abdominal wall • ligamentum teres hepatis • splenic artery • tail of the pancreas • short gastric arteries • left gastroepiploic vessels

question: The gastrosplenic ligament connects the spleen to the stomach and contains the {c1::short gastric arteries} and {c2::left gastroepiploic vessels}.
answer:
These vessels are branches of the splenic artery running within the gastrosplenic ligament.

Diagram Labels: Key Structures Shown: anterior abdominal wall • ligamentum teres hepatis • splenic artery • tail of the pancreas • short gastric arteries • left gastroepiploic vessels

question: The free margin of the lesser omentum contains the portal triad, which consists of the {c1::bile duct}, {c2::hepatic artery}, and {c3::portal vein}.
answer:
Mnemonic: 'VAD' from anterior to posterior in the free edge, or portal vein posterior, bile duct right, hepatic artery left.

Diagram Labels: Key Structures Shown: anterior abdominal wall • ligamentum teres hepatis • splenic artery • tail of the pancreas • short gastric arteries • left gastroepiploic vessels

question: The attached margin of the lesser omentum transmits the {c1::left gastric artery} and the {c2::right gastric artery}.
answer:
These arteries form an anastomotic arc along the lesser curvature of the stomach.

Diagram Labels: Key Structures Shown: anterior abdominal wall • ligamentum teres hepatis • splenic artery • tail of the pancreas • short gastric arteries • left gastroepiploic vessels

question: The epiploic foramen (Foramen of Winslow) acts as the direct communication between the greater sac and the {c1::lesser sac}.
answer:
Anterior boundary: Free margin of lesser omentum. Posterior boundary: IVC and right suprarenal gland.

Diagram Labels: Key Structures Shown: anterior abdominal wall • ligamentum teres hepatis • splenic artery • tail of the pancreas • short gastric arteries • left gastroepiploic vessels

question: The most dependent site of the peritoneal cavity in the supine position is the {{c1::hepatorenal pouch of Morrison}}.
answer:
High Yield: Bounded by the liver, right kidney, and colon. Fluid (ascites, blood, pus) readily accumulates here in supine patients.

Diagram Labels: Key Structures Shown: hepatorenal pouch of Morrison

question: In the sitting or standing position, the most dependent site of the peritoneal cavity in females is the {{c1::rectouterine pouch}} (pouch of Douglas).
answer: Clinically important for culdocentesis to aspirate fluid from the peritoneal cavity via the posterior vaginal fornix.

question: In the sitting or standing position, the most dependent site of the peritoneal cavity in males is the {{c1::rectovesical pouch}}.
answer: Located between the rectum and the urinary bladder.

question: The phrenicocolic ligament connects the {{c1::diaphragm}} to the {{c2::splenic flexure of the colon}}.
answer: High Yield: It supports the spleen inferiorly. In splenomegaly, this ligament directs the enlarging spleen medially and inferiorly toward the right iliac fossa.

question: The superiormost layer of the perineum that separates the pelvis from the perineum is the {{c1::pelvic diaphragm}}.
answer: Main components include levator ani and ischiococcygeus muscles.

question: The three main muscle components forming the levator ani are {{c1::pubococcygeus}}, {{c2::iliococcygeus}}, and {{c3::ischiococcygeus}} (coccygeus).
answer:
Provides essential pelvic floor support and maintains urinary and fecal continence.

Diagram Labels: Key Structures Shown: pubococcygeus • iliococcygeus • ischiococcygeus • puborectalis • pubourethralis • pubovaginalis

question: The specific part of the levator ani considered the 'muscle of continence' that maintains the anorectal angle is the {{c1::puborectalis}}.
answer:
Forms a sling around the anorectal junction, creating the acute perineal flexure crucial for fecal continence.

Diagram Labels: Key Structures Shown: pubococcygeus • iliococcygeus • ischiococcygeus • puborectalis • pubourethralis • pubovaginalis

question: Specific muscle modifications of the pubococcygeus include {{c1::pubourethralis}}, {{c2::pubovaginalis}}, and {{c3::puborectalis}}.
answer:
These fibers insert into or sling around respective pelvic viscera.

Diagram Labels: Key Structures Shown: pubococcygeus • iliococcygeus • ischiococcygeus • puborectalis • pubourethralis • pubovaginalis

question: Which specific perineal muscle is NOT a part of the perineal body? {{c1::Ischiocavernosus}}.
answer: Must-know NEET PG exception: Ischiocavernosus does not attach to the central tendon of the perineum (perineal body).

question: Among the muscles of the perineum, there are {{c1::4}} paired muscles and {{c2::2}} unpaired muscles.
answer: Paired: Superficial transverse perineal, deep transverse perineal, bulbospongiosus, levator ani. Unpaired: External anal sphincter, longitudinal muscle of anal canal.

question: The inferior layer of the urogenital diaphragm is also known as the {{c1::perineal membrane}}.
answer:
Spans the pubic arch and supports the deep perineal pouch structures.

Diagram Labels: Key Structures Shown: perineal membrane

question: The Inguinal Canal is 4 cm long, extends from the deep inguinal ring (defect in {{c1::fascia transversalis}}) to the superficial inguinal ring (defect in {{c2::external oblique aponeurosis}}).
answer:
Deep Ring Location: 1.25 cm above midinguinal point (midway between ASIS and pubic symphysis), immediately lateral to inferior epigastric vessels.

Diagram Labels: Key Structures Shown: fascia transversalis • external oblique aponeurosis • internal oblique • lateral • medial • outside

question: The Spermatic cord has 3 coverings: External spermatic fascia (from {{c1::external oblique aponeurosis}}), Cremasteric muscle & fascia (from {{c2::internal oblique}}), and Internal spermatic fascia (from {{c3::fascia transversalis}}).
answer:
Note: Transversus abdominis does NOT contribute a covering to the spermatic cord because it arches over it as the conjoint tendon.

Diagram Labels: Key Structures Shown: fascia transversalis • external oblique aponeurosis • internal oblique • lateral • medial • outside

question: Indirect inguinal hernia enters the deep ring {{c1::lateral}} to the inferior epigastric artery, whereas Direct inguinal hernia pushes through Hesselbach's triangle {{c2::medial}} to the inferior epigastric artery.
answer:
Hesselbach's Triangle Boundaries:
- Medial: Lateral border of rectus abdominis.
- Lateral: Inferior epigastric vessels.
- Inferior: Inguinal ligament.
Hernias here are direct and acquired due to weak fascia transversalis.

Diagram Labels: Key Structures Shown: fascia transversalis • external oblique aponeurosis • internal oblique • lateral • medial • outside

question: The ilioinguinal nerve enters the inguinal canal through the lateral wall and emerges through the superficial ring {{c1::outside}} the spermatic cord, supplying sensory to the anterior scrotum/labium majus.
answer:
Genital branch of Genitofemoral nerve: Runs INSIDE the spermatic cord and provides motor supply to the cremaster muscle (efferent limb of cremasteric reflex - L1, L2).

Diagram Labels: Key Structures Shown: fascia transversalis • external oblique aponeurosis • internal oblique • lateral • medial • outside

question: The Epiploic Foramen of Winslow connects the greater sac to the lesser sac (omental bursa) and is bounded anteriorly by the {{c1::portal triad (proper hepatic A., portal V., bile duct)}} in the free margin of lesser omentum.
answer:
Boundaries of Foramen of Winslow:
- Anterior: Portal triad in hepatoduodenal ligament.
- Posterior: Inferior vena cava (IVC) and right crus of diaphragm.
- Superior: Caudate lobe of liver.
- Inferior: First part of duodenum.

Diagram Labels: Key Structures Shown: portal triad (proper hepatic A., portal V., bile duct) • hepatic artery and portal vein

question: The Pringle maneuver compresses the hepatoduodenal ligament to temporarily control bleeding from the {{c1::hepatic artery and portal vein}}.
answer:

Diagram Labels: Key Structures Shown: portal triad (proper hepatic A., portal V., bile duct) • hepatic artery and portal vein

question: The Pouch of Douglas (rectouterine pouch) is the most dependent peritoneal space in females in the upright position, lying between the {{c1::posterior wall of uterus}} and {{c2::anterior wall of rectum}}.
answer:

Diagram Labels: Key Structures Shown: posterior wall of uterus • anterior wall of rectum

question: The deep perineal pouch is bounded superiorly by the superior fascia of urogenital diaphragm and inferiorly by the {{c1::perineal membrane}}.
answer:
Deep Pouch Contents (Males): Membranous urethra, Sphincter urethrae, Deep transverse perineal muscle, Bulbourethral (Cowper's) glands, and dorsal nerve of penis.

Diagram Labels: Key Structures Shown: perineal membrane • deep • spongy (bulbous) urethra • Scarpa's fascia • fascia lata

question: Bulbourethral (Cowper's) glands are situated in the {{c1::deep}} perineal pouch, but their ducts pierce the perineal membrane to open into the {{c2::spongy (bulbous) urethra}} in the superficial perineal pouch.
answer:
High Yield Classic Question: Location is in deep pouch; drainage is in superficial pouch.

Diagram Labels: Key Structures Shown: perineal membrane • deep • spongy (bulbous) urethra • Scarpa's fascia • fascia lata

question: Rupture of the bulbous urethra (straddle injury) causes extravasation of urine into the superficial perineal pouch, which can spread into the scrotum, penis, and lower anterior abdominal wall deep to {{c1::Scarpa's fascia}}, but CANNOT pass into the thigh due to attachment to {{c2::fascia lata}}.
answer:
Colles' Fascia: Membranous layer of superficial fascia of perineum, continuous with Scarpa's fascia anteriorly, attached to ischiopubic rami laterally and perineal body posteriorly.

Diagram Labels: Key Structures Shown: perineal membrane • deep • spongy (bulbous) urethra • Scarpa's fascia • fascia lata

question: The Pectinate (Dentate) line divides the anal canal into upper and lower parts: the upper part is derived from {{c1::endoderm (hindgut)}} and the lower part from {{c2::ectoderm (proctodeum)}}.
answer:
Pectinate Line Landmarks:
- Upper: Columnar epithelium, Superior rectal A. (IMA), Portal venous drainage, Internal iliac lymph nodes, autonomic innervation (painless hemorrhoids).
- Lower: Stratified squamous epithelium, Inferior rectal A. (Internal pudendal), Caval venous drainage, Superficial inguinal lymph nodes, Somatic pudendal innervation (painful hemorrhoids).

question: Internal hemorrhoids originate above the pectinate line, are covered by mucous membrane, and are PAINLESS because they are innervated by {{c1::autonomic (inferior hypogastric plexus)}} nerves.
answer: External Hemorrhoids: Lie below pectinate line, covered by skin, extremely PAINFUL due to somatic sensory supply by inferior rectal nerve (branch of pudendal nerve).

question: The external anal sphincter is innervated by the {{c1::inferior rectal nerve}} (branch of pudendal N., S2-S4) and the perineal branch of {{c2::S4}}.
answer: Internal Anal Sphincter: Involuntary smooth muscle (thickening of circular muscle layer); sympathetic (contractile - L1, L2) and parasympathetic (relaxing - S2-S4 via pelvic splanchnic nerves).

question: The Ischioanal (Ischiorectal) Fossa is bounded laterally by the {{c1::Obturator Internus}} covered by obturator fascia and medially by the {{c2::Levator Ani and External Anal Sphincter}}.
answer: Pudendal (Alcock's) Canal: Fascial canal in the lateral wall of the ischioanal fossa containing the pudendal nerve and internal pudendal vessels.

question: The Pelvic Diaphragm is formed by the {{c1::Levator Ani}} and {{c2::Coccygeus (Ischiococcygeus)}} muscles.
answer: Levator Ani Subdivisions: Pubococcygeus, Puborectalis (forms U-shaped sling maintaining anorectal angle at 80° for fecal continence), and Iliococcygeus.

question: The internal pudendal artery and pudendal nerve exit the pelvis through the {{c1::greater sciatic foramen}} below the piriformis, cross the ischial spine/sacrospinous ligament, and enter the ischioanal fossa through the {{c2::lesser sciatic foramen}}.
